title: The False Promise of Instructional Models
author: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones
summary: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones argues that whole-school instructional models, the lesson wheels and phase sequences many Australian schools adopt for consistency, cannot deliver what they promise. Her core point is that lesson design depends on what is being taught, so a model generic enough to span a poem, an equation and a tennis serve is blind to curriculum, and the same problem recurs even within a single subject such as music. She adds that structural consistency, like everyone running a Do Now, tells leaders nothing about the quality of the retrieval practice inside it, and that a rigid model can push skilled teachers to choose between effective practice and compliance. In its place she offers three better bets: invest in excellent shared curriculum, agree on instructional principles without prescribing exactly how they are applied, and specify routines where a strong case exists, such as paired fluency reading. She concedes that improving instruction this way is more demanding than imposing a lesson template, and ends with staffroom reflection questions on principles versus practices. This piece was expanded from Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #129.
points: Because a whole-school model must apply to every subject and year level, it is necessarily blind to the curriculum content that, following Christine Counsell, determines every pedagogical decision.
Even within one subject the instructional needs vary so much that a single model cannot fit, as the range of music lessons from notation to ensemble rehearsal shows.

Structural consistency can look like quality while saying nothing about how good the retrieval practice or explanation actually is, and a rigid model may force skilled teachers to choose compliance over effectiveness.
Jones's three priorities are excellent shared curriculum, agreed instructional principles held tightly but applied flexibly, and specified routines where a strong case exists for shared practice.
Her closing point is that real instructional improvement is inconveniently harder than adopting a template, since it demands curriculum investment and specific teacher knowledge.
quotes: Lesson models applied across a school are necessarily blind to the specifics of curriculum. This is not a small issue: it is a fundamental flaw. By design, instructional models must be sufficiently generic to apply across subjects, year levels, domains and subdomains.

Christine Counsell, whose writing on curriculum may be the best on the planet, reminds us that the curriculum “object” (the thing being taught) determines every pedagogical decision to follow. Instructional models, then, are the cart before the horse.

If a lesson model cannot accommodate lessons within a single subject, it seems absurd to expect an instructional model to accommodate the full breadth of a school’s curriculum. It truly is a false promise.

When we seek consistency through a common lesson model, we may indeed observe some comforting structural consistency. We walk the halls and see all students engaging in the “Do Now”, the first phase of the whole-school model. This tells us teachers are drawing on a repeatable structure, but it tells us nothing about the quality of retrieval practice being offered.

If we want to reduce unnecessary variation between classrooms, curriculum is the place to start. Teams of teachers should know exactly what they are teaching, when they are teaching it and how that content connects to what students have learned and will learn next.
We needn’t present these principles in a Canva wheel of death, because agreeing on instructional principles does not require prescribing exactly when or how they must be applied.
This is where schools can make real progress: developing teachers’ expertise in high yield practices, alongside their judgment about when to use them, for what purpose and under what conditions.

Improving instruction is inconveniently more demanding than implementing a school-wide lesson structure. It requires schools to invest in curriculum quality, develop teachers’ instructional knowledge in specific ways and to flexibly implement well-codified, shared techniques.
